title: Why Don't Woodpeckers Get Headaches? 🐦
description:
Woodpeckers hammer trees up to 20 times a second at over 1,000 g, so why don't woodpeckers get brain damage or headaches? A 2022 slow-motion study found the skull is a stiff hammer, not a shock absorber, and their tiny brains can handle far bigger hits than ours.

Sources:
https://www.npr.org/2022/07/14/1111577543/why-dont-woodpecker-brains-get-damaged-from-pecking-theyre-tiny-scientists-say

script: Woodpeckers headbang trees twenty times a second, and you'd be out cold after one. So why don't they get headaches? Each peck stops the head in about a thousandth of a second. That's over a thousand g. For years, people thought the skull was a spongy crash helmet. But in 2022, slow-motion videos showed it barely cushions anything. It's a stiff hammer, because a soft one would hit weaker. The real trick is size. A woodpecker's brain weighs just a few grams, packed so snugly it barely sloshes. Tiny brains handle far bigger hits than ours. Plus, its long tongue bone wraps all the way around its skull, which may help keep things steady. That's up to twelve thousand pecks a day, and not one headache. So what would you headbang twenty times a second?
key_facts: Woodpeckers can peck up to about 20 times a second
Each strike decelerates the head in roughly a millisecond, at over 1,000 g
A 2022 high-speed video study (Van Wassenbergh et al., Current Biology) found the skull acts as a stiff hammer, not a shock absorber
A woodpecker brain weighs only a few grams and fits snugly, and small brains tolerate much higher decelerations
The hyoid (tongue bone) wraps around the skull; its protective role is debated
Some woodpeckers peck about 12,000 times a day
